documents: Published paper: Gleason et al. 2022, Ultrafast structural response of shock-compressed plagioclase, Meteoritics & Planetary Science 57(3), 635-643 (HAL deposit hal-04946741; PDF with HAL cover page, journal pages 635-643)

entry.evidence: The pressure at which amorphization begins and the process by which it occurs is the subject of ongoing debate.

steps.action: Pose the debated question of the onset pressure and the pathway of shock amorphization of plagioclase, which matters for shock barometry.
steps.quote: The pressure at which amorphization begins and the process by which it occurs is the subject of ongoing debate.

steps.action: Take the published rivals from other groups: a hollandite-type high-pressure polymorph inferred from velocimetry, with a mixed-phase regime above the ~5 GPa HEL; optical evidence placing the start of amorphization near 15 GPa.
steps.quote: Ahrens et al. (1969) used velocimetry to suggest the transformation of plagioclase to a high-pressure polymorph

steps.action: Design a laser-shock pump / XFEL XRD probe test on synthesized polycrystalline labradorite (An52.5) wafers behind a 15 µm plastic ablator, with transmission XRD and VISAR; sample synthesis and setup are given in Methods.
steps.quote: Polycrystalline plagioclase wafers were prepared by loading ground labradorite into 2 mm outer diameter Pt tubes

steps.action: Set the conditions in the laboratory by shock-compressing samples at LCLS-MEC to a range of pressures and probing at chosen time delays with 50 fs, 8 keV X-ray pulses.
steps.quote: were shock compressed at the matter in extreme conditions (MEC) end station

steps.action: Estimate the pressure for each shot from XRD lattice parameters and/or VISAR particle velocities through equations of state, and report the average with the standard deviation as uncertainty.
steps.quote: For each shot, the pressure was determined using a combination of XRD to measure crystalline lattice parameters for unit cell volumes

steps.action: Check the premises of the pressure and timing measurements: VISAR runs on thinner samples extrapolated to zero thickness to account for shock decay, XRD calibration against NIST CeO2 and LaB6, and oscilloscope verification of time delays (Methods only).
steps.quote: Additional VISAR data, measuring particle velocities, were collected on thinner samples to determine the pressure at intermediate positions.

steps.action: Record XRD at full compression: crystalline at 3(1) GPa, diffuse scattering appearing at 8(2) GPa, and only diffuse signal at 32(10) GPa.
steps.quote: crystalline peaks are still present, but a diffuse feature has started to develop.

steps.action: Interpret the peak broadening and diffuse scattering as amorphization, while naming nanocrystalline formation, loss of periodicity, and stress gradients as possible causes of the broadening.
steps.quote: We interpret the increase in peak FWHM and formation of diffuse features in the XRD as amorphization of plagioclase.

steps.action: Compare the amorphization onset with the mixed-phase regime above the HEL inferred from earlier velocimetry, and find them consistent.
steps.quote: [...] amorphization coincides with the start of the mixed-phase regime just above the ~5 GPa HEL

steps.action: Infer, qualitatively, a loss of medium-range order and a rise in Si/Al coordination from the pressure trend in the intensity ratio of the two diffuse features (Fig. S2), noting that the limited Q-range prevents a structure-factor analysis.
steps.quote: increase in cation coordination number, wherein the sixfold coordination of silicon and aluminum increases

steps.action: Compute the diffraction peaks expected from the rival crystalline high-pressure phases (hollandite-, clinopyroxene-, and zagamiite-type model phases with EoS) for comparison with the highest-pressure trace.
steps.quote: A qualitative comparison of calculated model phases

steps.action: Exclude formation of a crystalline hollandite-type polymorph (lingunite/stöfflerite) because none was observed on compression or release.
steps.quote: none of these crystalline minerals were observed in our experiments during either the compression or release stages.

steps.action: Argue from crystal chemistry and kinetics that reconstructive polymorph formation is inhibited on shock timescales, so a metastable amorphous phase is expected.
steps.quote: atomic motion to thermodynamically preferred positions is kinetically inhibited, resulting in a metastable amorphous phase.

steps.action: Exclude melting on release as the source of the amorphous phase, using published entropy-density and density-pressure data that require ~50 GPa for melt.
steps.quote: compression to ~50 GPa is necessary to produce melt upon release.

steps.action: Compare the result with Jaret et al. (2015) on maskelynite ordering and find it corroborated.
steps.quote: findings on maskelynite, also observing a notable degree of disordering at long length scales upon compression

steps.action: Establish from time-resolved series at 8(2), 15(3), and 32(10) GPa that the same behavior repeats at all pressures above the HEL.
steps.quote: Notably, the behavior is similar for all shock pressures above the HEL, indicating a unified mechanism

steps.action: Observe on release the shift of the diffuse feature to larger d-spacing (HDA to LDA), followed by recrystallization into the original structure by 100 ns.
steps.quote: LDA glass formation is followed by recrystallization back into the original structure at extended time delays.

steps.action: Compare the recovery (memory effect) with static diamond-anvil-cell results; argue that the critical pressure is higher under dynamic loading because of strain rate.
steps.quote: is consistent with static diamond anvil cell results

steps.action: Observe that samples shocked to 8(2) and 15(3) GPa recover crystallinity sooner, at ~25-30 ns.
steps.quote: The recovery of crystallinity appears sooner for plagioclase shocked to pressures below its critical point.

steps.action: Explain the earlier recovery by remnant long-range periodicity lowering the barrier to recrystallization.
steps.quote: the remnants of long-range periodicity should enable a lower energetic barrier to reform the primitive structure.

steps.action: Keep the claim that a memory effect exists at laser-shock timescales.
steps.quote: a memory effect exists even at the very short timescale of laser shock compression.

steps.action: Reconcile the conflict with ex situ optical studies (amorphous material only above ~15 GPa) by an auxiliary: post-shock recovery via the memory effect erases the low-pressure amorphous material.
steps.quote: An apparent inconsistency with optical studies that only report amorphous material in excess of ~15 GPa

steps.action: Compare full amorphization at 32(10) GPa with the published ~45 GPa maskelynite threshold and judge them consistent.
steps.quote: the previously defined ~45 GPa threshold for maskelynite formation

steps.action: Refine the account into one continuous mechanism (Fig. 4): crystalline below the HEL, then a rising amorphous and HDA fraction with pressure, LDA on release, and morphology set by amorphous fraction and memory-effect recovery.
steps.quote: The structural composition of this high-pressure state varies continuously in two ways as pressure increases.

steps.action: Compare the mechanism with spectroscopic studies of Ries crater maskelynite.
steps.quote: showing maskelynite spectral features similar to fused feldspar, despite being recovered from extreme shock conditions.

steps.action: Keep the headline claim: direct conversion of plagioclase to an amorphous (maskelynite) phase without a crystalline high-pressure phase, beginning at ~5 GPa, with partial recrystallization on release.
steps.quote: revealing a 5 GPa onset pressure for amorphization, which is much lower than previously suggested.

tree.answer: Shock-induced amorphization of plagioclase (maskelynite formation) and its onset pressure
Yes, observed directly by in situ time-resolved XRD during shock
Determine the onset pressure and transformation pathway of shock amorphization
Cited crystalline high-pressure polymorph vs direct amorphization; melt on release; nanocrystals or stress gradients as causes of broadening
Polymorphs predict distinct Bragg peaks (calculated model phases); amorphization predicts diffuse scattering
Conditions set in the laboratory by laser shock at chosen pressures and time delays
Partly: pressure from two methods plus instrument checks; behavior repeats across three pressures; broadening rivals not tested
Kept: direct amorphization above the HEL, no crystalline polymorph, memory effect on release
No review file supplied (reviews by O. Tschauner acknowledged)

end.claim: Under laser shock, plagioclase amorphizes directly, without a crystalline high-pressure phase, starting just above the ~5 GPa Hugoniot elastic limit and fully amorphous at 32(10) GPa, and partially recrystallizes on release (memory effect).

decisive_move.sentence: The in situ XRD patterns at full compression, showing diffuse scattering from 8(2) GPa and a fully diffuse pattern at 32(10) GPa, are the evidence without which neither the low onset pressure nor the direct-amorphization claim would exist.

gates.evidence: Action: the experiment was aimed at the debated pathway (cited polymorph vs amorphization; onset at ~5 vs ~15 GPa), but no hypothesis is stated as directing shot pressures or delays. Claim: the crystalline-polymorph rival could have appeared as Bragg peaks and was not seen (p. 638), and amorphization could have begun only near 15 GPa. However, the broadening alternatives (nanocrystals, stress gradients) are named but not tested (p. 637), and the onset is bracketed only by shots at 3(1) and 8(2) GPa. Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data.

imports.item: X-ray free-electron laser (LCLS) femtosecond XRD probe
VISAR velocity interferometry with impedance matching through LiF/quartz windows
NIST CeO2 and LaB6 powder standards for XRD calibration
High- and low-density amorphous (HDA/LDA) polyamorphism and glass structural relaxation
Simon-Glatzel equation for extrapolating the melt curve

novelty_claims.quote: present the first structural study of plagioclase during shock compression
these results uniquely reveal that previously considered distinct shock stages are in fact derived from a single continuous mechanism.
Thus, we present the first in situ measurement of amorphization of plagioclase during shock [...] .
demonstrates, for the first time, that a memory effect exists even at the very short timescale of laser shock compression.
[...] direct conversion of plagioclase to maskelynite for the first time
The memory effect is seen for the first time during the shock release process

limits:
Documents: no review file or earlier version was supplied, although the acknowledgments thank O. Tschauner for reviews. The supporting information (Discussion S1, Table S1, Data S1, and the Fig. S1-S6 images) was not supplied; only the figure captions printed on p. 643 were read.

Process not shown:
- The number of shots, and how pressures and delays were chosen, are not reported.
- The 'Fig. 3d' cited on p. 639 is not among the panels shown (a-c) (inference: a figure-labelling error).
- The alternative causes of peak broadening (nanocrystals, loss of periodicity, stress gradients) are named but never tested or excluded.
- The onset 'just above 5 GPa' is bracketed only by shots at 3(1) and 8(2) GPa; the 5 GPa value is the cited HEL, not a measured onset.

Internal tensions:
- The Fig. 2 caption says the model-phase comparison suggests 'a zagamiite-type or hollandite-type topology forms', while the text says no crystalline polymorph was observed.
- The critical pressure is given as 32(10) GPa in the Results and as ~30-35 GPa in the Discussion.

Sub-claims and their statuses:
- Memory effect at nanosecond timescales: best_explanation, from observed recrystallization.
- Rise in cation coordination and loss of medium-range order: qualitative inference, status none; the authors note the limited Q-range.
- Single continuous mechanism (Fig. 4): best_explanation, an interpretive synthesis with the cited literature.
- Higher dynamic critical pressure due to strain rate: asserted, not tested.

Outcome: coded kept rather than contradicted, because the paper reconciles the earlier optical ~15 GPa onset as an apparent discrepancy (the memory effect) rather than showing those data wrong.

Composition is none_fits: the work is problem-driven and uses a new probe (as in capability_first), but the question and cited rivals come first. The crucial test (Bragg peaks vs diffuse scattering) excludes the polymorph rival, but it is not framed as a strong-inference design across all rivals, and no rival is refined.

disagreements.target: Previously assumed onset pressure of amorphization (~15 GPa mixed-phase start set from optical data)
disagreements.support: In situ XRD shows diffuse scattering already at 8(2) GPa, just above the HEL, while the 3(1) GPa pattern stays crystalline.
disagreements.quote: Direct amorphization begins at pressures much lower than what was previously assumed

disagreements.target: Ahrens et al. (1969) hollandite-type high-pressure polymorph inferred from velocimetry
disagreements.support: No crystalline polymorph peaks were seen on compression or release; a kinetic crystal-chemical argument favours a metastable amorphous phase.
disagreements.quote: none of these crystalline minerals were observed in our experiments

disagreements.target: Optical studies reporting amorphous material only above ~15 GPa (Cygan et al., 1989; Langenhorst, 1994)
disagreements.support: Time-resolved data show amorphization recovering to crystal on release, so ex situ observation would miss it.
disagreements.quote: An apparent inconsistency with optical studies that only report amorphous material in excess of ~15 GPa

disagreements.target: Static-compression critical pressure for recovery (Sims et al., 2020; Stöffler et al., 1991)
disagreements.support: Recovery is observed in shock experiments with an apparent critical pressure of 32(10) GPa, attributed to the different strain rate; this attribution is not tested.
disagreements.quote: The nature of dynamic compression lends itself to a higher critical pressure of 32(10) GPa due to the differing strain rate

disagreements.target: Classification of PDFs and maskelynite as distinct shock stages (Stöffler et al., 1991)
disagreements.support: The amorphous fraction rises gradually with pressure, read as one continuous mechanism in which the distinction is microstructural.
disagreements.quote: Thus, maskelynite may not be atomistically distinct from amorphous PDFs.

alternatives_considered.reason: to provide better fringe quality for highest pressure shots
